title: The Commissions: NHRC, NCW, NCSC, NCST, NCM, NCBC

cards.h: Watchdogs for rights and for vulnerable groups
cards.b:
Besides courts, India has a set of commissions to protect rights and particular groups: the NHRC (human rights), NCW (women), NCSC (Scheduled Castes), NCST (Scheduled Tribes), NCM (minorities) and NCBC (backward classes).

Some are constitutional (NCSC, NCST, NCBC); others are statutory (NHRC, NCW, NCM). This difference matters for status and permanence but less for power: all mainly investigate and recommend.

The exam question is usually: are they "toothless tigers"? You need their legal basis, composition, powers and examples of success or failure.

cards.h: Constitutional or statutory: a quick map
cards.b:
• Article 338 began as a Special Officer for SC and ST. The 65th Amendment (1990) made a multi-member commission. The 89th Amendment (2003) split it into NCSC (338) and NCST (338A, from 2004).
  • The NCBC was set up in 1993 by law after Indra Sawhney, and given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).

• Created by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, in line with the UN Paris Principles (1993) for national human rights institutions.
  • Chair: a former Chief Justice of India, or (since the 2019 amendment) a former Supreme Court judge. Members include judges and experts; ex-officio members are chairs of other national commissions.
  • Appointment: by the President on the advice of a committee of the PM, Speaker, Home Minister, Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses and the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman.
  • Powers: inquire into violations (on complaint or on its own), powers of a civil court for summons, visit jails, intervene in court cases, recommend compensation or prosecution.
  • Limits: its recommendations are not binding; it cannot look at complaints older than one year; on the armed forces it can only seek a report from the government (Section 19).

Justice V. Ramasubramanian became chairperson in December 2024. State Human Rights Commissions follow the same Act.

Positive record: guidelines on custodial deaths (to be reported within 24 hours), encounter killings (inquiry procedure), bonded labour, and the Gujarat riots of 2002, where it moved the Supreme Court for transfers of cases.

Criticisms:

  • Critics often call it a "toothless tiger", since it can only recommend.
  • Mostly retired judges and officers; few civil society members.
  • Staff and investigators come from the police.
  • The Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) deferred its "A" status review in 2023 and 2024, citing issues of pluralism, independence and the role of police in investigations.

Thinkers to cite: Upendra Baxi (The Future of Human Rights, 2002) on the gap between the rhetoric and the "politics of suffering".

• Composition: chairperson, vice-chairperson and three members, appointed by the President.
  • Duties (Articles 338, 338A): investigate safeguards, inquire into complaints, advise on development, and report to the President, who lays reports before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum.
  • Powers: of a civil court in inquiries.
  • The NCST also has duties on forest rights, displacement and the protection of tribal lands.

Context: they monitor the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and reservation. Problems: reports are often tabled years late, and many posts have stayed vacant for long periods. The commissions lack their own investigators.

Debates: creamy layer and sub-classification after Davinder Singh (2024); Dalit Christians and Muslims' demand for SC status (examined by the K.G. Balakrishnan commission set up in 2022).

• The NCBC Act, 1993 created it after Indra Sawhney to advise on inclusion and exclusion in OBC lists.
  • The 102nd Amendment (2018) repealed the Act and made it constitutional under Article 338B, with powers like the NCSC's to look into OBC grievances. Article 342A gave the President power to notify OBC lists.
  • In Jaishri Patil (Maratha case, May 2021), the Court read this as taking away states' power to identify OBCs. The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the states' power to keep their own lists.
  • The Rohini Commission (2017-2023) studied sub-categorisation of central OBC lists.

Debates: which castes to include (Jats, Marathas, Patidars), creamy layer income limit (₹8 lakh since 2017), and the coming caste data from Census 2027.

National Commission for Women

Set up in January 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990. A chairperson and five members (at least one from SC/ST). Reviews safeguards for women, inquires into complaints, recommends changes in law. It has influenced laws on dowry, domestic violence (2005) and sexual harassment at work (POSH Act, 2013). Critics say it reacts selectively and is close to the ruling party.

National Commission for Minorities

Statutory under the NCM Act, 1992. Six notified minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains (Jains added in 2014). Monitors safeguards and inquires into complaints. Grew out of the Minorities Commission of 1978. Critics point to vacancies and weak follow-up. The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions (2004) deals with Article 30 rights.

Related: the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (2005 Act, set up 2007).

Why "toothless":

  • Recommendations are advisory; government can ignore them.
  • Appointments are made by the executive, often from ruling party circles.
  • Delays, vacancies, and dependence on ministries for staff and money.
  • Overlap: several commissions may handle the same complaint.

Why still useful:

  • They create public records, guidelines and pressure.
  • They give victims a cheaper, quicker forum than courts.
  • Parliamentary reporting forces some response.

Reforms: binding powers on compensation, independent investigation teams, pluralist membership, fixed budgets, time limits on action-taken reports, and merging overlapping bodies. The Second ARC (2005-09) made similar points.

• Manipur (2023-26): commissions were criticised for slow responses to ethnic violence and sexual assault cases; the Supreme Court set up its own committee of former judges (August 2023).
  • NHRC accreditation: GANHRI's deferrals (2023-24) became a reputational issue.
  • Caste census: Census 2027 data will matter for NCBC and NCSC work.
  • Waqf Act 2025 and minority rights claims before the NCM and courts.
  • Custodial deaths and encounter cases continue to reach the NHRC.

"National commissions are toothless tigers. Critically examine with reference to the NHRC."
"Compare the constitutional and statutory status of the commissions for SCs, STs and backward classes."
"Evaluate the role of the National Commission for Women."

Structure: map of bodies and their legal basis; NHRC composition and powers with Paris Principles; record and limits; NCSC, NCST, NCBC with amendments (65th, 89th, 102nd, 105th); NCW, NCM; critique and reforms; recent cases; balanced conclusion.
